newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN seeks safety guarantee for Cambodian Ranariddh.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN seeks safety guarantee for Cambodian Ranariddh.

text.p: ASEAN wants Cambodian co-premier Hun Sen to guarantee the safety of his ousted rival as part of a regional peace package for the strife-torn country, diplomatic sources said on Thursday.

The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) was set to take on a mediation mission after Second Prime Minister Hun Sen apparently changed his mind to say he would welcome an ASEAN mediation role.
Hun Sen's ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in a bloody coup in early July caused ASEAN to withhold Cambodia's scheduled admission this week.
After rebuffing the group's attempts to mediate in the crisis, Hun Sen said on Thursday that ASEAN could play a role in ensuring Cambodia's stability.
"The stability of Cambodia -- we need the role of ASEAN," he said in Cambodia's capital city of Phnom Penh. He also said he was not upset by the deferral of Cambodia's membership into ASEAN.
ASEAN now comprises Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
The diplomats who studied briefing notes for the mediation effort said ASEAN would insist on several other conditions, including:
-- Cessation of all hostilities, including alleged political violence against Ranariddh's followers;
-- Restoration of the coalition government, but not necessarily with Ranariddh as its head;
-- Elections be held as scheduled in 1998;
-- The maintenance of the country's institutions as they existed before the coup, including the monarchy, the National Assembly and the Constitution.
The main sticking point would appear to be ASEAN's insistence that Ranariddh be allowed to return safely to Cambodia.
Hun Sen has accused him of treason, saying he was making a deal with the reviled Khmer Rouge faction and bringing in arms and soldiers into the capital of Phnom Penh.
The deposed co-premier has been jetting around the region to try to drum up support from other countries. He is set to meet his father, King Norodom Sihanouk, in Beijing.

Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot, who is attending the ASEAN meetings as head of his country's observer delegation, said in a speech to the opening session of the ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting that elections would be held next year.
"The UN and independent observers are cordially invited to participate as observers," he said.

Ung Huot also said key state institutions would remain in place, including the monarchy under King Sihanouk, the constitution, the principles of liberal democracy, and the 1991 Paris Peace Accords that ended Cambodia's two-decade old civil war.
He said the National Assembly would reconvene on July 28.
Ung Huot did not mention any safety guarantees for Ranariddh or his followers in the royalist FUNCINPEC party.
He said the fighting that erupted in the capital on July 5-6 was due to the entry of "hard-core and hard-line Khmer Rouge soldiers".
"It was not a so-called coup d'etat as has been alleged, but a legitimate action to prevent Cambodia from slipping into anarchy and a possible second genocide," he said.
It was still not entirely clear whether Hun Sen was sincere in his acceptance of an ASEAN mediation role, diplomats said.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, who led a three-member ASEAN mission last week to Phnom Penh, was furious after Hun Sen's caustic and abrupt dismissal of the mediation offer, diplomats said.
The United States, one of Cambodia's biggest foreign aid donors, said it was co-ordinating its mediation efforts with ASEAN.
Solarz, President Bill Clinton's special envoy, arrived on Thursday in Phnom Penh as part of his Asian diplomatic shuttle on Cambodia.
The former congressman told reporters in Thailand on Thursday that Washington was encouraged by Hun Sen's latest reaction to ASEAN's mediation offer.
